blocks.text: Vol. I, book 1, Chapter 1, p. 1. I shall add the words that bear on this: "Just as an animal is called ζῶον [zōon] in Greek, so in Hebrew it is called חיה by reason of life. Not that in the view of the Hebrews life is proper to the animal, as the learned think. For Aben Ezra and Ramban, on the first chapter of Genesis, acknowledge that there is life in plants. And this is clear from Scripture, when it promises that men shall live like grain, Os. XIV, 7. To which the Apostle alludes, 1 Cor. XV, 36. Accordingly trees are said to be killed and to die, that is, to be deprived of life. Thus Ps. LXXVIII, 47: He killed their vines with hail. On these words Kimchi says: גם יתכן בצומח מיתה אחר אשר בו נפש הצומחת, Death also befits a plant, since there is a vegetative soul in it. Hence Horace, book 1, Epist. 12: But whether you slaughter fish, or leek and onion. And Seneca, Epist. 58: For it is held that crops and shrubs have a soul: and so we say that they both live and die. To the same point are these words of Job about a tree, ch. 14, v. 8: Though its root grow old in the earth, and its stock die in the dust. And the outcry of the Egyptians to Joseph, Genes. XLVII, 19: Why should we die before you, both we and our land? For the land is said to die when it lies uncultivated and desolate, since it lives in some way in its produce. Hence Martial, book 13, Epigr. 12: — — lest the suburban field should die. And Statius, book 5 of the Thebaid, on the serpent by which Archemorus was killed: — the grass, struck by its hot breath, falls where it bore its jaws; the field dies at its hissing. Therefore that the plant lives is admitted among the Hebrews too. But because the animal alone feels, desires and moves, life is sometimes attributed to it as its own, since it rises many degrees above the life of the plant."

The carcasses of locusts also infect the air with stench and noxious exhalations, so that evil diseases arise. JEROME, in his Commentary on Joel, Chapter 2, on the swarms of locusts that infested Palestine in his time: When the shores of both seas were filled with heaps of dead locusts, which the waters had cast up, their putrefaction and stench was so harmful that it corrupted the air as well, and a pestilence arose among beasts as well as men. ATHANAS. KIRCHER, in Scrutinium physico-medicum contagiosae luis, Leipzig 1659, p. 43: There can be no plainer sign of an epidemic sickness soon to follow than swarms of locusts flying through the summer. FRID. HOFFMANN, in Medicina Systematica, T. II, vol. II, ch. 4, §. 14: In the year 1692 an incredible quantity of locusts was seen flying in the air, which infested all Thuringia, Meissen and the Vogtland, and, descending to the ground, did very great damage to the crops and vegetation; from which time many malignant fevers, indeed fevers joined with petechiae, began to rage in these regions. IGNAC. DE ASSO confirms this very thing with several testimonies in the book often cited, Chapter 2, p. 12–15, German trans.

THEVENOT, Travels, vol. I, p. 12: Heavy rains kill the locusts. — The Cossacks are freed from locusts only in this way, unless perhaps, after they have begun to fly, the north wind or the Corus carries them off into the Black Sea. HASSELQUIST himself saw at Smyrna great swarms of locusts hurled into the sea by the wind, Itin. p. 253. 254.

Nothing, however, prevents us from understanding the east wind in this passage, since Arabia, because of its deserts and its sandy and barren hills, especially favours the breeding of locusts (Cf. OEDMANN, Histor. Nat. Arabiae petraeae, in his Vermischte Sammlungen, Fasc. 6, ch. 24, p. 176), and even now many swarms of them are often carried from Arabia both into Eretz Yisrael and Syria and into Egypt.
